title: Jonah Runs From God
overview: God sends Jonah to warn Nineveh, Jonah sails the other way, and a storm at sea brings his escape to a sudden end.

parts.label: Called and running away (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Nineveh was a leading city of Assyria, a powerful and feared empire that was Israel's enemy, far to the east. Jonah instead sails for Tarshish, likely a distant western port, and later in the book (4:2) he admits he ran because he expected God to show Nineveh mercy.

parts.label: Storm and a sleeping prophet (vv. 4-6)
parts.note: The text presents the storm as sent by the LORD, aimed at the ship carrying Jonah. While the sailors pray to their own gods and throw cargo overboard, Jonah sleeps deep below deck, and the captain has to tell the prophet to pray.

parts.label: The lot falls on Jonah (vv. 7-10)
parts.note: Casting lots was something like drawing straws, a common ancient way of seeking a divine answer, and many people then believed one guilty person could bring disaster on everyone near him. Jonah calls his God the maker of sea and land, so the sailors are terrified to learn he is fleeing the very God behind the storm.

parts.label: Thrown into the sea (vv. 11-16)
parts.note: Jonah tells them to throw him overboard, but the sailors first row hard for shore and then pray not to be blamed for his death. When the sea goes calm, these foreign sailors end up honoring the LORD with a sacrifice and promises, more readily than the prophet himself.

parts.label: The great fish (v. 17)
parts.note: The text says only a huge fish, not a whale, and presents it as the LORD's way of keeping Jonah alive rather than ending him. Christians read the three days and nights as pointing to Jesus' time in the tomb, since Jesus made that comparison himself (Matthew 12:40).

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Jonah is meant to be read as a literal historical account or as a true-to-life story told to teach about God's mercy toward outsiders.
think: What makes it harder to want good things for people we see as enemies than to face danger ourselves?
